[UPDATE:  4/24-28/2026]
Changed tactic - realized that finding the "overlapping" references probably misses references to older works, so went back into "02" and generated the list of UNIQUE references from both columns of "refs".  In item 3 below (and the corresponding code chunk), I've documented my logic and how I found those works from the "refs_filt_unique" that do NOT appear in the dataframe once I filter the works down to just those works that appear in the "unique" refs list.

I also edited Step 4 to investigate the primary topic fields of the new "works" df.  On 4/28/2026, I looked at the new subfield distributions.

I have NOT edited any of the commentary or code from BEFORE item 3 or AFTER item 4.



The data subsetting step of this project was an iterative process.  After initially subsetting based on language, type, retraction, and publication year, and removing those with blank values for the title, I wanted to explore several other attributes of the data.  

1) NA values for either the primary topic or fwci - I then filtered the "filt_works" object based on this exploration 


```{r Data Exploration - "works_filt" - NA removal}

print(count(works_filt, is.na(fwci)))  # 2:        TRUE  10694
print(count(works_filt, is.na(primary_topic)))  # 2: TRUE   10680  
print(count(works_filt, is.na(primary_topic_subfield)))  # 2: TRUE   10680
print(count(works_filt, is.na(primary_topic_field)))  # 2: TRUE   10680
print(count(works_filt, is.na(primary_topic_domain)))  # 2: TRUE   10680

#  after filtering out the NA values for "primary_topic" - all the "primary_topic_..." variables have no NA values
# and "fwci" only has 14 values, so I'll filter those out 
# can see from Global Environments it worked - now there are 131409 observations

```

3) Verification that intersecting the filtered works with the UNIQUE references worked.  

This step used %in% to select just those observations in the the "works_filt" object that are found in the "refs_unique" object.  But the number of observations of the new object did NOT match the number in the list of unique references; the following code shows how the intersection was verified.

(Prior to using the %in% approach for this step, I tested the different types of joins to see if either of them seemed like a better option.  That code is in the "02_bibliometrics_data_subsetting_tests" rmd.)


```{r need to find the 1634 citations from the unique references that aren't in the filtered works}

refs_to_join <- refs_unique %>% 
  select(work_id = citation)

joined_refs_works <- full_join(works_filt, refs_to_join, by = "work_id")

nrow(joined_refs_works)  # [1] 104709
nrow(joined_refs_works) - nrow(filt_works)  # [1] 1634

print(count(joined_refs_works, is.na(work_id)))  # 1:  FALSE 104709 (so no NA values in the work_id)
print(count(joined_refs_works, is.na(source_id)))   # 2: TRUE     1634

missing_refs_only <- joined_refs_works %>%
  filter(is.na(source_id))

# I want to explore these manually
# need to write a csv and do this in Excel

refs_not_in_works <- works %>%
  filter(work_id %in% missing_refs_only$work_id)

output_directory <- "C:/Users/Owner/Documents/Research/R_Projects/nais_ps/data_output/"
file_name <- "Refs_not_in_Works_v2.csv"
full_output_path <- file.path(output_directory, file_name)

write_excel_csv(refs_not_in_works, file = full_output_path)

# OK, found them!  
# in the spreadsheet, I highlighted why each would have been filtered out
# so, should definitely use either the %in% or one of the joins that does NOT keep the "refs" that aren't in the "works"

```

Step 9) As part of considering whether or not to filter based on the different "primary_topic*" variables, I also wanted to assess the distribution of "Indigenous" specific language in both the title and primary topic.  Takeaway:  In the filtered works that appear in the overlapping list of references, there are 56 observations that have "Indigenous|indigenous|tribal|tribe|Tribe|Native") in either the title or primary topic field - which equates to 0.28% of the works.  (In the full list of filtered references, including those not found in the overlapping references, there are 2860 observations - which equates to 2.8%.)

It might be interesting to take a much closer look at teh 56 articles from the filter/overlapped works.  

```{r tallying "Indigenous"}

# run 1:  BEFORE limiting the "filt_works" to just those that appear in the overlapping reference list
  ## each command starts by piping in "filt_works" 

# run 2:  AFTER limiting the "filt_works" to just those that appear in the overlapping reference list
  ## each command starts by piping in "filt_overlap_works" 

# in the "filter" line:
  # space between the different calls is OK - BUT! - 
  # do NOT include a space between the different terms of each "str_detect" call

indig_title_topic_or <- works_filt %>% 
  # filter(str_detect(primary_topic, "Indigenous|indigenous|Tribal|tribal|Tribe|tribe|Native")) %>%  
  filter(str_detect(title, "Indigenous|indigenous|Tribal|tribal|Tribe|tribe|Native") | 
           str_detect(primary_topic, "Indigenous|indigenous|Tribal|tribal|Tribe|tribe|Native")) %>%
  group_by(primary_topic_field) %>%  # group_by(primary_topic_field)
  summarise(n_Indig = n())
```
